newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD tries to force the pace on tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: German SPD tries to force the pace on tax cuts.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), looking ahead to general elections next year, sought on Friday to outflank the ruling coalition's plans to slash income tax in 1999 by calling for earlier cuts.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said reform plans announced by Finance Minister Theo Waigel would punish workers, pensioners and Germany's four million unemployed. Despite the criticism, he called for urgent cross-party talks on tax cuts.

"We want to see a real impact on people's wallets in 1998, and not just promises of tax cuts for 1999," Lafontaine said. He warned that if Chancellor Helmut Kohl wins election for a record fifth term his government would break its tax pledges.
Kohl's chief tax strategist, Christian Democrat (CDU) parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble, dismissed Lafontaine's attack, but gave a guarded welcome to the offer of talks.
"The coalition is ready at any time to hold meaningful talks with the SPD on the tax reforms. But they must be serious," Schaeuble said in a statement.

The SPD chief was reacting to plans announced by Waigel to slash income and corporate taxes while scrapping 70 tax breaks in measures that would leave taxpayers 30 billion marks ($18 billion) better off. Most of the cuts would come in 1999.

The reforms would bring in new bottom income tax rate of 15 percent, to be followed by a sliding scale running from 22.5 percent to 39 percent. Corporate taxes would fall in two steps with a final top rate of 35 percent.
Waigel wants to raise the 15 percent rate of value-added tax by a point to finance the cuts, but the SPD is threatening to veto a rise in parliament's upper house, which it controls.

SPD finance spokesman Karl Diller said the tax cuts would push state borrowing over the Maastricht Treaty limit of three percent of gross domestic product required for European economic and monetary union.
"Waigel's tax cuts on tick will endanger monetary union," Diller said.
Plans to raise taxes on pensions and life insurance have also split Kohl's CDU. Labour Minister Norbert Bluem was among a minority of party leaders who voted against the tax plan.
Kohl has ordered a cooling-off period before his party looks at VAT again next month. Party sources said he read the riot act to Bluem at a party meeting on Thursday.
While industry groups welcomed the plan's goal of slashing corporate taxation, some lobby groups were hostile.
Trade unions said that the abolition of tax breaks would hit the poor hardest, while the wealthy would win out from the lower top rate of tax.

That view was backed up by a survey by the Forsa institute which found that 62 percent of Germans thought they would not profit from the reform. Sixty-four percent thought the rich would benefit most. The survey sample was 500 people.
Commentators were also critical, with the Handelsblatt daily saying Waigel had fallen short of his earlier goal of cutting top income tax to 35 percent from today's 53 percent.
"It is understandable that the coalition is trying to sell the tax reform as the work of the century. But its is not a convincing showpiece," Handelsblatt remarked.
The tax proposals face a long road before they become law.
Legislation is only expected to be introduced to parliament this summer. If the SPD blocks the measures a compromise may be delayed into early 1998 -- with autumn polls already looming.
